newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Shoppers get relief from dogged salesmen.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Shoppers get relief from dogged salesmen.

text.p: To many American shoppers, commissioned sales clerks are like lost dogs. Once you make eye contact, you're stuck with an unwanted friend.

But consumers who are tired of pushy salesmen are getting some relief. The commission system that shoppers have come to associate with electronics superstores, car dealerships and large department stores is undergoing major revision.
As consumers pick and choose from a wider selection of stores than ever before, some of the country's retailers are finding that commissions turn off their customers and cost more than they're worth.

Companies such as Best Buy Co. Inc. Good Guys Inc. and department store retailer Macy's all have created new pay formulas that rely less heavily on straight commissions but still inspire workers to ring up a lot of merchandise. Similarly, automakers such as Saturn have adopted a no-haggle approach to car sales.

For a long time, America's retailers tried to mimic Nordstrom Inc., whose commissioned sales force is widely saluted as one of the best. What makes Nordstrom and other commissioned salesmen successful is their ability to get a customer's attention without a hard sell.

Even though Eleanor King, who has sold appliances for almost a decade at Sears, Roebuck and Co., depends on her commission paychecks to pay her mortgage, she's no vulture. With her soft push and large clietele, King rang up $950,000 last year and is shooting for $1 million this year.
"It can be tough," said King, a 34-year-old single mother of two teenage girls. "There are a lot of people I know who are afraid of commission pay."

At Sears, appliance department workers make roughly a four to five percent cut on sales. But Sears, like many other retailers, pays commissions only to some of its workers. And now many store chains are discovering they can boost customer service without surrendering a slice of sales to employees.

Instead of paying commissions, these retailers are offering bonuses and gifts to workers who bend over backwards to please shoppers. And in some cases, sales people prefer this form of compensation to the mad swings of commission pay.

"I think we're becoming much more sophisticated about the level of service that the customer expects and that we should provide," said Jim Andress, senior vice president of human resources for Macy's East Coast division. "So we're tailoring to a greater degree where we pay commission."
Consumer electronics megastore Best Buy tinkered with its compensation formula this year in hopes of boosting sales of fat-profit appliance products and reducing its dependency on low-margin PCs.
Seven years ago, the Minneapolis-based company stopped paying its workers commissions when it transformed from a 40-store regional chain to a warehouse retailer in 31 states.

While it has not revived commissions, it is testing a system in which appliance department workers share a team bonus if they meet sales goals. The chain also is carrying popular gourmet kitchen gadgets and staffing the department with permanent workers instead of relying on floaters with less knowledge about products.

Best Buy has not yet decided whether to roll out team bonuses throughout the company, but this change and others already are paying off. Manufacturers that were once skittish about selling their name-brand white goods in Best Buy's self-serve stores are again doing business with the chain.

Nick Johnson, a Best Buy store manager in Fairlakes, Virginia, said group bonuses make more sense than commissions because employees focus on pleasing customers rather than achieving personal financial goals.
"I was very glad to get out of it," said Johnson, 31, who worked as a salesman for the company before it scrapped commissions. "If you didn't sell, you didn't eat."
Finding workers who can handle the seasonal ups and downs of non-salary pay is a big challenge for retailers, experts said.

"The retention rate is a real problem," said Martin Leestma, a partner with Andersen Consulting LLP. "That's what every retailer in America's running into: "How do I retain good employees and be the preferred place to work, specifically at the younger ages.'"
Macy's department store recently dropped commissions for about 60 percent of the workers in 17 of its 88 East Coast stores after deciding they just didn't pay.

Macy's workers have greeted the change warmly, the New York-based retailer said. Now, instead of watching their paychecks gyrate with swings in consumer confidence, workers take comfort in the predictability of an hourly wage. Their pay now is based on an average of their earnings over the past 12 months, plus opportunities for bonuses.
"They couldn't be happier right now," said Macy's Andress. "In effect, we've taken all the risk away," at least until the next performance review.

The shift has had no measurable impact on sales. It has, however, produced payroll savings for Macy's, which expects to trim staffing levels. It has also eliminated one expense because poor-performing workers often left the company before selling enough merchandise to cover pay advanced by the firm, leaving Macy's with a deficit.

San Francisco-based Good Guys revised its compensation system when Best Buy was preparing to invade California about two years ago. After polling shoppers, the retailer decided it needed to beef up customer service. So instead of rewarding workers just when they rang up a sale, it also began paying a bonus when shoppers return for a second purchase.

"Consumers assume all sales people are bad," said Bob Baird, vice president of merchandising. "They start out with the notion that whoever is going to come up and talk to them is bad. So we have to break through that."
